newsitem.title: USA: SEC adopts rules lifting hedge fund restrictions.
newsitem.headline: SEC adopts rules lifting hedge fund restrictions.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission approved Thursday rules that ease restraints on private investment companies, including hedge funds and venture-capital businesses.

The rules, which go into effect in 60 days, would lift restrictions on how many investors these often high-risk, but high-return funds can accept, as long as those investors meet certain qualifications.
"This is an important segment of our securities markets, and the rules we consider today are likely to make these private funds even more important in the future," said SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt.

Under current SEC rules, such funds are limited to 100 investors, but Congress last year mandated changes to allow more investment in these private investment vehicles, absent the SEC's regulatory reporting requirements.
SEC officials anticipate the new rules will allow companies and other entities to more easily raise capital.
"Hedge funds, venture capital pools, and other privately offered investment companies can be a source of seed money for promising but capital-starved start-up businesses," Levitt said.

The rules are good news for the securities industry, according to Robert Todd Lang, a senior partner of the New York Law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges who also serves as co-chairman of the American Bar Association's task force on hedge funds.
"This reform really is overdue," Lang said. "This is going to over time expand capital formation and it's going to help smaller companies."

Under the rules, these private funds would be relieved of SEC reporting requirements as long as investors in the fund are individuals with at least $5 million in investments, institutions with at least $25 million in investments, or private companies with $50 million in equity.
That would include some retirement plans as well as certain state and local government pension plans.
However, SEC officials made clear that not all participants in 401K and other retirement plans with $25 million in investments would automatically qualify to invest in these private funds.
SEC Commissioner Steven Wallman cautioned that determining whether or not retirement benefit plans are qualified to make such investments is going to be an important issue.
"I think this is a growing area and a growing area of confusion," Wallman said.
